question:
Undo doesn't emit `notified_changed` signal in a GTK/Python application

I am trying to develop a PyGObject application but experiencing a strange behavior. I’ve created a demo for you to reproduce it. This is the code: import gi gi.require_version("Gtk", "4.0") from gi.repository import Gtk, Gio app = Gtk.Application() window = None text_view = None title = "Test" def on_quit(action, _): app.quit() def on_save_file(action, _): text_view.get_buffer().set_modified(False) def create_action(target, name, handler): action = Gio.SimpleAction(name=name) action.connect("activate", handler) target.add_action(action) def add_actions(app, window): create_action(app, "quit", on_quit) create_action(window, "save_file", on_save_file) def set_accels_for_actions(app): app.set_accels_for_action("win.save_file", ["<Ctrl>s"]) app.set_accels_for_action("app.quit", ["<Ctrl>q"]) def on_modified_changed(buffer): modified = buffer.get_modified() print("Modified:", modified) if modified: window.set_title(f"{title}*") else: window.set_title(title) def on_activate_app(app): global window, text_view window = Gtk.ApplicationWindow(application=app) text_view = Gtk.TextView() text_view.get_buffer().connect("modified_changed", on_modified_changed) window.set_child(text_view) window.present() add_actions(app, window) set_accels_for_actions(app) app.connect("activate", on_activate_app) app.run() You can quit from app using "Ctrl+q" and save the content with "Ctrl+s". Just do this: * Write "a". * Delete it with "Backspace". * Write "b". * Press "Ctrl-s" and save it. It is not a real save, just calls `buffer.set_modified(False)`. You can follow the `modified` flag value in the co
llm_attempt: GTK4's built-in TextView undo (Ctrl+Z/Ctrl+Y, enabled via the buffer's default enable-undo=True) replays edits through an internal history mechanism that doesn't always route through the same code path that flips GtkTextBuffer's modified flag, so "modified-changed" can fail to fire after undo even though the buffer content actually changed. Don't rely on "modified-changed" alone to track dirty state around undo/redo. Instead, connect to the buffer's "changed" signal (which fires on every content mutation, including undo/redo) and manage your own dirty flag there, e.g. compare against a saved baseline text/hash, or explicitly call buffer.set_modified(True) inside the "changed" handler if it isn't already true. Also confirm you're on a recent GTK4 point release, since undo/modified-tracking interactions have had fixes across 4.x versions. You can also watch buffer.get_can_undo()/get_can_redo() transitions as a supplementary signal around undo actions.

But if I try to switch to a page that was displayed before in the current runtime, it is just not displayed until I do one of the following: If I click outside the application (desktop, for example), the page will be displayed correctly. I want to share what I did so people encountering this bug have a (hacky) solution at least. If it is against guidelines to post this as an answer, please let me know. So what I found out is the following: giving Frames an event bind for <Enter> or <Leave> does not help on its own. The binding has to trigger a configure on an element (only tested it with .configure(bg="color") so maybe other uses of configure do not work). I created a widget like this: import tkinter as tk class Updater(tk.Frame): def __init__(self, parent, height, width) # ececec is the default frame color under OSX 10.13.6 tk.Frame.__init__(self, parent, height=height, width=width, bg="#ececec") self.grid_propagate(False) self.bind("<Enter>", self.triggerDisplay) self.bind("<Leave>", self.triggerDisplay) def triggerDisplay(self, event): self.configure(bg="#ececec") Then I put a 1x1 wide version of this widget onto every one of my pages in the topmost left corner. The effect is that the page will display instantly if the mouse pointer enters or leaves the topmost left corner (0,0). I then simply added a method to the class that handles page transitions, which moves the mouse pointer to (0,0), being the topmost left corner of the page, like this: def moveToCorner(self): self.update_idletasks() self.event_generate("<Motion>", warp=True, x=0, y=0) Lastly, I call moveToCorner() on every page transition, and my application displays pages like it should. If the code contains typos, it's because I typed it by hand (b
llm_attempt: This is a known Tk/Aqua redraw bug on older macOS Tk builds: grid_remove() followed by grid() changes geometry but Tk fails to invalidate the drawing region until some other event (focus, Enter/Leave, click) forces a repaint. The robust fix is to stop using grid_remove()/grid() for page switching and instead keep all page frames gridded into the same cell permanently, switching visibility with tkraise(): place each page once with frame.grid(row=0, column=0, sticky='nsew'), then call frame.tkraise() to switch pages. Since the frame never leaves the geometry manager, there's no remove/re-add redraw path to trigger the bug. If you must keep grid_remove()/grid(), try forcing a redraw afterward with widget.update_idletasks(), root.update(), or a dummy event_generate('<Configure>'), and consider testing with a newer Tcl/Tk (8.6.x) build rather than whatever ships with the old system Python, since this class of repaint bug was fixed in later Tk releases.

question:
Transformers 'could not import module pipeline' to jupyter notebook

I need to to run a series of pre-trained fine-tuned models from Hugging Face to Jupyter notebook. I have updated to the latest version of both PyTorch and Transformers, but when I run the code from transformers import pipeline pipe = pipeline("text-generation", model="abeja/ABEJA-QwQ32b-Reasoning-Japanese-v1.0") messages = [ {"role": "user", "content": "Who are you?"}, ] pipe(messages) Instead of transformers loading the model I get a long error message ending in: "ModuleNotFoundError: Could not import module 'pipeline'. Are this object's requirements defined correctly?" I have tried uninstalling and re-installing PyTorch and Transformers, and running the command as from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM instead, but nothing's worked so far. The kernel path is currently /Users/Library/Jupyter/kernels/python3 . The only other thing that I can think of as significant is it's being run off a Mac Mini M4...I can't see how the hardware would be an issue but have heard people say there can be problems running LLMs on a Mac Mini...
llm_attempt: That message is transformers' lazy-import wrapper hiding the real exception: "pipeline" itself imports fine, but something it depends on for this task/model failed to import, and the generic LazyModule error masks the actual traceback. Get the real error by importing directly: from transformers.pipelines import pipeline in a fresh cell, or set TRANSFORMERS_VERBOSITY=debug / run in a plain terminal to see the full stack above the final line. Common causes: missing optional deps for this specific model (try pip install accelerate sentencepiece protobuf tiktoken), a torch build mismatch (on Apple Silicon make sure you have the arm64 wheel, not an x86 one under Rosetta - check python -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.backends.mps.is_available())"), or the Jupyter kernel pointing at a different Python/env than the one you installed packages into (check sys.executable vs. where pip installed). Reinstalling torch/transformers rarely fixes this if it's actually a missing optional dependency for that particular model's pipeline class.

question:
Difference in Measuring Latency of (torch.)Multiprocessing.Queue

I'm writing a program that requires transferring GPU tensors across processes in a pipeline manner. I knew that using torch.Multiprocessing would automatically get the CudaIpcMemHandle for me and send it through the pipe under the hood of Multiprocessing.Queue. I wanted to measure the latency of each item go through the Queue. I implemented this code main_high.py : The method is when the producer put an item to the Queue, it will also add a timestamp time.perf_counter_ns() in the tuple being sent through Queue. import csv import os import time from typing import Dict, List, Tuple import torch import torch.multiprocessing as mp def producer(queue: mp.Queue, num_items: int) -> None: # float32 uses 4 bytes per element -> 5 MiB tensor. num_elements = (5 * 1024 * 1024) // 4 tensor_bytes = num_elements * torch.tensor([], dtype=torch.float32).element_size() print(f"[producer] creating a new tensor per item, size={tensor_bytes} bytes") for item_index in range(num_items): tensor = torch.rand(num_elements, dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda") # Ensure tensor materialization is complete before starting transfer timing. torch.cuda.synchronize() ts_start = time.perf_counter_ns() print(f"start time, item {item_index}: {ts_start} ns") queue.put(("data", item_index, tensor, ts_start)) del tensor queue.put(("done",)) def consumer(in_queue: mp.Queue) -> None: item_count = 0 producer_done = 0 latencies_ms = {} while True: item = in_queue.get() ts_end = time.perf_counter_ns() if item[0] == "done": break _, item_index, tensor, ts_start = item latency_ms = (ts_end - ts_start) / 1e6 latencies_ms[i
llm_attempt: With CUDA tensors through torch.multiprocessing.Queue, put() only sends the CUDA IPC handle (metadata) - actual GPU memory isn't copied synchronously, so a naive time.perf_counter_ns() wrapped around put/get mostly measures Python pickling plus pipe/IPC-handle transfer time, not real data-transfer latency, and CUDA calls are asynchronous by default so timings can be misleading unless you synchronize at the right points. You already call torch.cuda.synchronize() on the producer before starting the timer, which is correct; you should also call torch.cuda.synchronize() on the consumer right after queue.get() before stamping ts_end, since reconstructing the tensor from the IPC handle doesn't guarantee the data is complete without a sync. For more accurate GPU-side latency, prefer torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True) recorded at send/receive and read via elapsed_time(), rather than wall-clock perf_counter, since that isolates device-side timing from OS scheduling/serialization noise in the Queue itself.

question:
Replace elements in a List column with multiple other elements

Consider the following DataFrame: df = pl.DataFrame({ "a":[ ["55", "87.19"], ["55.11","55.12"], ["55", "27.89"] ] }) I would like to replace all "55" with "55.11", "55.12" . That is, I would like the end result to be: df = pl.DataFrame({ "a":[ ["55.11","55.12", "87.19"], ["55.11","55.12"], ["55.11","55.12", "27.89"] ] }) How can I achieve that?
reference_answer: Here's something similar to my answer in this question (thanks jqurious for the heads up) df.select(pl.col("a").list.eval( pl.when(pl.element() == "55") .then(pl.lit(["55.11", "55.12"])) .otherwise(pl.concat_list(pl.element())) .explode() )) Or, a regex way, inspired by this answer to the same question df.select( pl.col("a").list.join("|") # replace "55" followed by "|" or the end of the string (captured) # replace with "55.11|55.12" followed by the captured character .str.replace_all(r"55(\||$)", "55.11|55.12$1") .str.split("|") ) Or, a more verbose / less elegant solution, that assigns a row id, explodes the list, replaces "55", and then groups the data back into lists ( df.with_row_index() .explode("a") .with_columns( pl.when(a = "55") .then(pl.lit(["55.11", "55.12"])) .otherwise(pl.concat_list("a")) .alias("a") ) .group_by("index") .agg(pl.col("a").explode()) .drop("index") )
llm_attempt:
list.eval can't fan one element out into several (it's strictly element-to-element), so replacing "55" with two values requires exploding the list, doing the replacement row-wise, then re-aggregating back into a list per original row:

mapping = {"55": ["55.11", "55.12"]}
out = (
    df.with_row_index("_idx")
      .explode("a")
      .with_columns(
          pl.col("a").map_elements(lambda x: mapping.get(x, [x]), return_dtype=pl.List(pl.Utf8))
      )
      .explode("a")
      .group_by("_idx", maintain_order=True)
      .agg(pl.col("a"))
      .drop("_idx")
)

This preserves row order and correctly expands "55" into ["55.11","55.12"] wherever it appears, leaving other elements untouched. For large data, a pure-expression version avoiding the Python map_elements callback would be faster (pl.when/then plus a second explode), but explode -> transform -> explode -> group_by is the general idiom for any 1-to-many replacement inside a List column in Polars.

question:
Cannot Keep My Datetime Data and 'No' Word in My Pandas DataFrame

I have a pandas dataframe from csv and I want to clean it using Regex in Python. The data that I have look like this: Name Date Status Number A/bCDef 2022-07-11 Yes io123-07 GhIjK-l 2022-07-12 No io456-08 I'm trying to clean the dataframe so it will be easier to process, but the thing is, my code deletes the date, the word 'no', and the hyphen. This the data that I got so far: name date status number abcdef yes io ghijkl no io This is the code that I found on the internet and tried on my dataframe: def regex_values(cols): nltk.download("stopwords") stemmer = nltk.SnowballStemmer('english') stopword = set(stopwords.words('english')) cols = str(cols).lower() cols = re.sub('\[.*?\]', '', cols) cols = re.sub('https?://\S+|www\.\S+', '', cols) cols = re.sub('<.*?>+/', '', cols) cols = re.sub('[%s]' % re.escape(string.punctuation), '', cols) cols = re.sub('\n', '', cols) cols = re.sub('\w*\d\w*', '', cols) cols = re.sub(r'^\s+|\s+$', '', cols) cols = re.sub(' +', ' ', cols) cols = re.sub(r'\b(\w+)(?:\W\1\b)+', 'r\1', cols, flags = re.IGNORECASE) cols = [word for word in cols.split(' ') if word not in stopword] cols = " ".join(cols) return cols This is the pandas dataframe that I wish to have at the end: name date status number abcdef 2022-07-11 yes io123-07 ghijkl 2022-07-12 no io456-08 I'm new to Regex so I wish anyone can help me to code the right code. Or if there is a simpler way to clean my data I would much appreciate the help. Thanks in advance.
reference_answer: can you try this: df = df.applymap(lambda s: s.lower() if type(s) == str else s) #lower string values df.columns = df.columns.str.lower() #lower for columns df['name']=df['name'].str.replace(r'\W+', '') #remove any non-word character #output ''' name date status number 0 abcdef 2022-07-11 yes io123-07 1 ghijkl 2022-07-12 no io456-08 '''
llm_attempt: The problem is that regex_values is far too aggressive for a whole-row cleanup: cols = re.sub('\w*\d\w*', '', cols) strips out any token containing a digit, which is exactly what destroys your Date and Number columns, and NLTK's English stopword list actually includes the word "no", so your stopword filter removes it too. The fix isn't a better regex, it's scoping the cleaning to the right column: only run regex_values on the free-text Name column, and leave Date and Number completely untouched - df['Name'] = df['Name'].apply(regex_values). For Status, don't stopword-filter at all - just df['Status'] = df['Status'].str.lower() - or if you reuse the same function, remove "no" (and "yes") from the stopword set first with stopword.discard('no'). Applying one generic "clean everything" function to structured columns like dates/IDs/status flags is the root mistake; treat each column according to what it actually contains instead of running every column through NLP-style text cleaning.

question:
Why is Jax treating floating point values as tracers rather than concretizing them when nesting jitted functions?

I am doing some physics simulations using jax, and this involves a function called the Hamiltonian defined as follows: # Constructing the Hamiltonian @partial(jit, static_argnames=['n', 'omega']) def hamiltonian(n: int, omega: float): """Construct the Hamiltonian for the system.""" H = omega * create(n) @ annhilate(n) return H and then a bigger function def solve_diff(n, omega, kappa, alpha0): that is defined as follows: @partial(jit, static_argnames=['n', 'omega']) def solve_diff(n, omega, kappa, alpha0): # Some functionality that uses kappa and alpha0 H = hamiltonian(n, omega) # returns an expectation value When I try to compute the gradient of this function using jax.grad n = 16 omega = 1.0 kappa = 0.1 alpha0 = 1.0 # Compute gradients with respect to omega, kappa, and alpha0 grad_population = grad(solve_diff, argnums=(1, 2, 3)) grads = grad_population(n, omega, kappa, alpha0) print(f"Gradient w.r.t. omega: {grads[0]}") print(f"Gradient w.r.t. kappa: {grads[1]}") print(f"Gradient w.r.t. alpha0: {grads[2]}") it outputs the following error: ValueError: Non-hashable static arguments are not supported. An error occurred while trying to hash an object of type <class 'jax._src.interpreters.ad.JVPTracer'>, Traced<ShapedArray(float32[], weak_type=True)>with<JVPTrace> with primal = 1.0 tangent = Traced<ShapedArray(float32[], weak_type=True)>with<JaxprTrace> with pval = (ShapedArray(float32[], weak_type=True), None) recipe = LambdaBinding(). The error was: TypeError: unhashable type: 'JVPTracer' Though, running solve_diff(16,1.0,0.1,1.0) on its own works as expected. Now if I remov
reference_answer: The fundamental issue is that you cannot differentiate with respect to a static variable, and if you try to do so you will get the error you observed. This is confusing me, because I no longer know what qualifies as static or dynamic variables anymore, from the definition that static variables does not change between function calls In JAX, the term "static" does not have to do with whether the variable is changed between function calls. Rather, a static variable is a variable that does not participate in tracing, which is the mechanism used to compute transformations like vmap , grad , jit , etc. When you differentiate with respect to a variable, it is no longer static because it is participating in the autodiff transformation, and trying to treat it as static later in the computation will lead to an error. For a discussion of transformations, tracing, and related concepts, I'd start with JAX Key Concepts: transformations .
llm_attempt: static_argnames=['n', 'omega'] on hamiltonian requires omega to be a concrete, hashable Python value at trace time. That's fine when you call solve_diff directly, but grad(solve_diff, argnums=(1,2,3)) differentiates with respect to omega, so JAX passes a JVPTracer for omega into solve_diff, which forwards it into hamiltonian - where it hits the static-argument machinery and fails to hash. An argument can't simultaneously be "static" (a fixed Python value known at trace time) and "differentiated" (traced). Fix: drop 'omega' from static_argnames on hamiltonian (and on solve_diff if you differentiate w.r.t. it there too), keeping only 'n' static, since n is a genuine shape/structural parameter that's never differentiated. omega should just be a normal traced float argument; jit handles that fine, it will simply retrace when omega's abstract shape/dtype changes, not on every value.

question:

"processors": [ { "inference": { "model_id": ".elser_model_2_linux-x86_64", "input_output": [ { "input_field": "content", "output_field": "content_embe
llm_attempt: Reindex's failures array only reports bulk-indexing failures, not ingest-pipeline processor failures - if the inference processor has (or defaults to) ignore_failure: true, or a preceding processor swallows errors via on_failure, documents can silently skip embedding generation while the reindex task still reports full success. Check the pipeline definition for ignore_failure/on_failure on the inference processors, and check _nodes/stats/ingest/pipelines plus the ELSER trained model stats (GET _ml/trained_models/.elser_model_2_linux-x86_64/_stats) for inference errors, queue timeouts, or rejected requests - ELSER deployments have limited allocations/threads, and under bulk load some inference calls can time out or get throttled rather than erroring loudly. Also check whether the affected documents actually have non-empty content/name source fields, since a missing/empty input field is commonly skipped without an error. Try _ingest/pipeline/elser_double_embedding_pipeline/_simulate against a few docs missing embeddings, and consider increasing model number_of_allocations/threads and re-running with slower throughput.

question:

reference_answer: This was indeed a bug which has now been fixed in release 3.2.12: https://github.com/dynaconf/dynaconf/issues/1367
llm_attempt: This looks like Dynaconf's environment-layer merge logic colliding with @get-resolved lists: when an @get token resolves to a list (calendar_ids) at a path nested underneath tables built up across [default]/[nonprod]/[prod] layers, Dynaconf's dict-merge machinery can treat the list as something to merge key-by-key against whatever structure already exists there, turning it into an index-keyed dict ({'0': 'a', '1': 'b'}) instead of leaving it as a plain list. This is a known rough edge in how Dynaconf merges Box/list structures across environments combined with lazily-resolved @get tokens, not something wrong in your TOML syntax - your carrot branch, which reads "@get google" as one top-level get rather than assembling nested tables plus per-field @gets, avoids it. Workaround: resolve the whole sub-object with one @get (like carrot does) rather than rebuilding the same shape field-by-field with nested tables, or check the latest Dynaconf issue tracker, since list-vs-dict merge handling is a recurring bug area there.

question:
How to remove the title bar of a tkinter application without making it full-screen or removing the taskbar icon?

I'm developing a tkinter application and would like to remove the title bar while keeping the window border intact and preserving the taskbar icon. Setting the window to full-screen or hiding the taskbar icon isn't desirable for my application. I've tried solutions involving overrideredirect(True) , but this removes both the title bar and the window border. Is there a way to achieve this on Windows (and ideally cross-platform) while still allowing the window to be resizable and draggable? Edit: from tkinter import Tk mroot = Tk() mroot.title("Welcome!") mroot.wm_attributes('-type', 'splash')
llm_attempt:
overrideredirect(True) removes window-manager decoration entirely, including the taskbar association, which is why you lose the taskbar icon. On Windows, strip just the caption/title bar while keeping the resizable border and taskbar icon by editing the native window style with ctypes after creation:

import ctypes
GWL_STYLE = -16
WS_CAPTION = 0x00C00000
hwnd = ctypes.windll.user32.GetParent(root.winfo_id())
style = ctypes.windll.user32.GetWindowLongPtrW(hwnd, GWL_STYLE)
ctypes.windll.user32.SetWindowLongPtrW(hwnd, GWL_STYLE, style & ~WS_CAPTION)
root.geometry(root.geometry())

This keeps WS_THICKFRAME (resizable border/drag) and the taskbar's WS_EX_APPWINDOW association intact, since only the caption bit is cleared rather than replacing the whole style like overrideredirect does. You'll need to implement your own drag-to-move (bind mouse events on a custom top strip), since removing the caption also removes native window dragging. This is Windows-specific - there's no single cross-platform tkinter API for partial decoration removal; each OS would need its own native-call approach.

question:
Dash Plotly Flask Application randomly hangs for 1 minute

I have build a simple application with two pages (a multi-page Dash app) which I am running locally using Gunicorn with two workers and four threads. It's a simple dashboard application. When I refresh the page in the browser and inspect the network tab, it usually takes 800ms to fetch the data and render it to the chart. The _dash-update-component typically takes about 800ms to respond and finish. However, there are instances when I reload the page and the same process suddenly takes about one minute. During this time, the page stays completely white and only shows the text "Loading...". This behavior is also visible in the Chrome network logs: Has anyone experienced this or have an idea what might be causing this?
reference_answer: gunicorn app:server --workers 4 --threads 1 --timeout 120 For CPU-heavy or Pandas/NumPy tasks, threads don’t help because of the Python GIL. Increasing worker and reducing threads improves responsiveness: 1.
llm_attempt: Intermittent ~60s stalls with Gunicorn sync workers usually mean a request got queued behind a thread/worker blocked on something synchronous - a slow or hanging outbound call (DB, API, file I/O) without a timeout, or lock contention on a shared global object (a requests.Session, DB connection, cache, matplotlib state) that isn't actually thread-safe across your 4 threads. Since it's occasional rather than constant, also check whether Gunicorn's worker --timeout (default 30s) is killing and respawning a worker mid-request, which can look like a ~60s hang to the browser (kill + retry). To isolate it: add timestamped logging at the start/end of each callback and around outbound calls, watch Gunicorn's logs for worker timeout/restart lines during a slow reload, and check whether the stall correlates with a specific callback (e.g. a network/DB fetch without an explicit timeout). If it's lock contention, moving to gthread with more workers (fewer threads each) or isolating the shared resource behind a proper connection pool usually resolves it.

question:
Pythonic way to obtain dictionary keys with desired property

In python 3.12 I have a dictionary of which the keys are 2-tuples of integers and of which the values are integers (as in the function f : N × N → N for which f ( n , m ) = n + m ). What I need is those keys of the dictionary where the first element has a specific value. It's simple enough to write a function like def matching_keys(d: dict[tuple[int, int], int], n: int) -> list[tuple[int, int]]: """ find all the keys in a dictionary *d* whose first element is the integer *n* :param d: the dictionary in question :type d: dict[tuple[int, int], int] :param n: the first-element value *n* in question :type n: int :return: a list of all the keys whose first elements are *n* """ result: list[tuple[int, int]] = [] for x,y in d.keys(): if x == n: result.append((x,y)) return result But it seems to me not particularly pythonic to write my own loop that checks each key explicitly. Is there a different way that's idiomatic (and perhaps not so imperative)?
reference_answer: You've overengineered it. Just do a list comprehension. matching_keys: list[tuple[int, int]] = [k for k in d if k[0] == n] Alternatively, unpacking is fine - actually preferable if you need to make sure len(k) == 2 at runtime: matching_keys: list[tuple[int, int]] = [(x,y) for (x,y) in d if x == n]
llm_attempt:
A list comprehension is the idiomatic replacement for that loop:

[key for key in d if key[0] == n]

That's already about as pythonic as it gets for a one-off filter - Python doesn't have a built-in dict-key-query mini-language beyond comprehensions/filter(). If you need to query by first element repeatedly for many different n values, it's more efficient to build an index once rather than rescanning the whole dict each time:

from collections import defaultdict
index = defaultdict(list)
for key in d:
    index[key[0]].append(key)

then index[n] is an O(1) lookup. For a single ad-hoc query, just use the comprehension - writing matching_keys as "return [key for key in d if key[0] == n]" is fine and arguably clearer than the explicit accumulator loop, since it says directly "give me the keys matching this predicate" rather than describing the mechanics of building the result list.

question:
How to annotate a function that takes a type annotation as an input and apply it to the output?

I want to type-annotate a function that takes a valid type annotation as an input parameter and returns a value that is type-annotated with the same annotation. It must support not just instances of type , but also special forms such as unions of multiple types or annotated types. (Under the hood, the function is converting the value to the given type via Pydantic. In the example below the untyped value is the input_value parameter, but in the real code it's returned by an API.) I want the following code to work: from typing import Annotated, Any, TypeVar, overload from typing_extensions import assert_type from pydantic import TypeAdapter T = TypeVar("T") @overload def convert(value: Any) -> Any: ... @overload def convert(value: Any, output_type: type[T]) -> T: ... def convert(value: Any, output_type: type[T] | Any = Any) -> T: adapter = TypeAdapter(output_type) return adapter.validate_python(value) assert_type(convert(1), Any) assert_type(convert(1, int), int) assert_type(convert(1, int | str), int | str) # "assert_type" mismatch: expected "int | str" but received "Unknown" assert_type(convert(1, Annotated[int, "foo"]), Annotated[int, "foo"]) # Argument of type "Annotated" cannot be assigned to parameter "output_type" of type "type[T@convert]" in function "convert" # Type "Annotated" is not assignable to type "type[T@convert]" # "assert_type" mismatch: expected "int" but received "Unknown" However this only works for values of output_type that are actual type objects, not type annotations in general. With pyright it fails with the inline errors shown above. Other type chec
llm_attempt: This is a real gap in the current typing system, not something you're doing wrong: type[T] only binds T when the argument is an actual class object, but unions, Annotated[...], and other special forms aren't instances of type - they're separate special-form objects - so type checkers can't infer T through them via a plain type[T] parameter. There's no stable, checker-portable annotation today for "a type expression that may be a class, union, or Annotated form, and bind T to what it denotes." There's an active typing-spec proposal (discussed as TypeForm/TypeExpr, roughly PEP 747) to add exactly this kind of annotation, but checker support is limited/experimental as of now, so you can't rely on it broadly yet. Practically: keep your overloads for type[T], accept that unions/Annotated inputs won't infer T precisely in pyright/mypy today, and use cast() at the call sites needing the special-form cases, or track that proposal's adoption if you need this to type-check cleanly long-term.

question:
Scrapy Crawlspider does not work with 507 status code

I have a scrapy Crawlspider that parses reviews, using a scrapy-rotating-proxies. But when I tried to connect to the site I got the 507 status code. In spite of that, I managed to connect to the site with the code 200 and get the information for a few times. As I understood the idea, the status 507 indicates the server does not have enough capacity to process the request. Or was I blocked after all? Is there anything I can do in this situation? I really need to get the data. My spider: class PagesCrawlSpider(CrawlSpider): name = "pages_crawl" allowed_domains = ["otzovik.com"] start_urls = ["https://otzovik.com/clothes_and_footwear/footwear_male/sports_shoes_for_men/"] rules = (Rule(LinkExtractor(restrict_xpaths="//div[@class='caption']/h3/a"), callback="parse_item", follow=True),) def parse_item(self, response): item = {} item["brand"] = response.xpath('//div[@class="page-caption"]/h1[@class="product-name"]/span/span[@class="fn"]/text()').get() item["plus"] = response.xpath('//div[@class="review-body-wrap"]/div[@class="review-plus"]/text()').getall() item["minus"] = response.xpath('//div[@class="review-body-wrap"]/div[@class="review-minus"]/text()').getall() return item Middlewares.py DOWNLOADER_MIDDLEWARES = { "rotating_proxies.middlewares.RotatingProxyMiddleware": 450, } ROTATING_PROXY_LIST_PATH = "{MY_PATH}/rotating_proxy_list.txt" Result scrapy crawl pages_crawl -o review_pages.json 2025-05-03 15:41:06 [scrapy.utils.log] INFO: Scrapy 2.12.0 started (bot: review_pages) 2025-05-03 15:41:06 [scrapy.utils.log] INFO: Versions: lxml 5.4.0.0, libxml2 2.11.9, cssselect 1.3.0, p
reference_answer: When I tried to access the site I immediately ran into a CAPTCHA. Once I had solved the CAPTCHA it became apparent that you'd need to at least provide some headers and cookies to access this site. This will retrieve the page that you are looking at: import requests cookies = { 'ROBINBOBIN': '3c0b88598a10dd0df58780b3c0', } headers = { 'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Ubuntu; Linux x86_64; rv:137.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/137.0', } params = { 'capt4a': '3211746332487724', } response = requests.get( 'https://otzovik.com/clothes_and_footwear/footwear_male/sports_shoes_for_men/', cookies=cookies, headers=headers, params=params, ) You'll need to integrate the headers, cookies and URL parameters into your Scrapy code. Hope this helps!
llm_attempt: 507 here is very unlikely to be a literal "server out of disk space" - it's far more common for anti-bot/WAF layers (or an overloaded origin behind a CDN) to return unusual 5xx codes as a soft block signal once they detect scraping/rotating-proxy traffic. First confirm what's actually in the 507 response body/headers (fetch it in a browser or curl through the same proxy) rather than assuming genuine capacity exhaustion. Then: add 507 to RETRY_HTTP_CODES (it isn't retried by default) alongside RETRY_ENABLED; slow down and randomize timing with AUTOTHROTTLE_ENABLED=True and a lower CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN; rotate User-Agent together with your proxies, not just IP, since blocking is often keyed on the combination; and check whether your rotating-proxy pool is low-quality/shared/already-blacklisted, which is the most common real cause of a scraper getting blocked intermittently even though manual/browser requests succeed. If none of that helps, the site is likely fingerprinting beyond IP+UA and you may need a headless-browser approach instead of raw Scrapy requests.

question:
Matplotlib yticks are not rising consecutively

import pandas as pd df = pd.DataFrame(data) print(df) #%% import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from matplotlib.ticker import MaxNLocator import numpy as np plt.scatter(df['time'], df['mag'], s=25, alpha=.3) plt.xlabel("Time") plt.ylabel("Magnitude") plt.xticks(df['time'], rotation=60) plt.gca().xaxis.set_major_locator(MaxNLocator(nbins=20)) plt.gca().yaxis.set_major_locator(MaxNLocator(nbins=30)) plt.show() So this is the code of my plot and since my df has a huge amounts of data I had some overlapping problem but fixed it with MaxNLocator. Now my y ticks look like the one in the photo but I want them to start from 2 and end with the highest. How can I do it?
reference_answer: Make sure that column is numeric and not string. df['mag'] = df['mag'].astype(float) Try setting your y axis plt.scatter(df['time'], df['mag'], s=25, alpha=.3) plt.xlabel("Time") plt.ylabel("Magnitude") plt.xticks(df['time'], rotation=60) y_min = 2 y_max = df['mag'].max() plt.ylim(y_min, y_max) plt.gca().xaxis.set_major_locator(MaxNLocator(nbins=20)) plt.gca().yaxis.set_major_locator(MaxNLocator(nbins=30)) plt.show()
llm_attempt:
MaxNLocator picks its own "nice round number" tick positions within your data range - it doesn't know you want the first tick to be exactly 2, it just fits roughly N evenly, aesthetically-spaced ticks. To force the y-axis to start at a specific value, set explicit ticks instead of (or in addition to) the locator:

import numpy as np
ymin, ymax = 2, df['mag'].max()
plt.gca().set_ylim(ymin, ymax)
plt.gca().set_yticks(np.arange(ymin, np.ceil(ymax) + 1, step))

pick step to match how many ticks you want. set_ylim(bottom=2) alone will clip the axis but MaxNLocator can still choose a first tick below/above 2 rounded to its own "nice" step; only set_yticks with an explicit array guarantees the first tick is exactly 2. If you want auto-chosen intervals but anchored at a fixed start, MaxNLocator doesn't support an anchor point - matplotlib.ticker.IndexLocator(base=step, offset=2) is the locator built for evenly-spaced ticks starting from a fixed offset.

I'm trying to make a whitelist where only certain roles can use this command, and it logs a role as being "theirs", I have tried debugging by printing roles and stuff and now It is not even going through the check, like it will print the admin table, but then doesn't move onto the check where it adds to the db/sends a message, it does nothing. cogs/roles.py import discord from discord.ext import commands from utils.databases import roles_db from utils.variables import admin class Roles(commands.Cog): def __init__(self, bot): self.bot = bot @commands.hybrid_group() async def custom(self, ctx: commands.Context): return @custom.command(name="register", description="Registers a custom role to a user") async def register(self, ctx: commands.Context, role: discord.Role, member: discord.Member): print(admin) if any(r.id in admin for r in ctx.author.roles): roles_db.insert_one({"user_id": member.id, "role_id": role.id}) await ctx.send(":white_check_mark: Role registered!") else: await ctx.send(":x: You do not have the required role.") async def setup(bot): await bot.add_cog(Roles(bot)) utils/variables.py admin = [ 1408442799925235794, 1445017368123277460 1079504634772738078 1272691594591473695 1379137477192843264 ]

question:
Creating an exponential moving average using StatefulDoFns in apache-beam but keep running into TypeError: 'float' object is not iterable

First question posted on stackoverflow so don't hesitate to give suggestions as to what tags to use for my post etc. I am trying to write an apache beam pipeline which imports timeseries data from a REST API and calculates an exponential moving average for each consecutive datapoint. Lastly, I would like to write this back into a REST API, but that is currently not the issue. For reference, see my code implementation below. import argparse import logging import os import apache_beam as beam from apache_beam.transforms.userstate import BagStateSpec, ReadModifyWriteStateSpec, TimerSpec, on_timer from apache_beam.transforms.timeutil import TimeDomain from apache_beam.utils.timestamp import Timestamp from apache_beam.utils.windowed_value import WindowedValue from apache_beam.transforms.trigger import AfterCount, AccumulationMode, Repeatedly from apache_beam.transforms.window import GlobalWindows, Duration, TimestampedValue import typing from apache_beam.typehints.decorators import with_input_types, with_output_types import requests from apache_beam.options.pipeline_options import PipelineOptions from typing import Union # Configure logging logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) logger = logging.getLogger(__name__) # Load environment variables django_container_name = os.getenv("DJANGO_CONTAINER", "django") django_port = os.getenv("DJANGO_PORT", "8000") def run(argv=None): # Parse command-line arguments parser = argparse.ArgumentParser() args, beam_args = parser.parse_known_args(argv) # Define custom pipeline options class MyOptions(PipelineOptions): @classmethod def _add_argpar
reference_answer: One issue that I see is that the BagState actually stores an iterable but it looks like you are treating it as a single value. previous_ema_value = previous_ema.read() ... ema = (element * alpha) + (previous_ema_value * (1 - alpha)) Since you always clear the bag and add a single value to it, a better fit for your use case is ValueState . But I do not think this is the cause of the error message you are seeing.
llm_attempt: "float object is not iterable" in a stateful EMA DoFn almost always means something is trying to iterate over the value read from a ReadModifyWriteStateSpec cell as if it were a collection. ReadModifyWriteStateSpec stores and returns a single value (your running EMA float) via state.read() - you use it directly (current = state.read() or initial_value), you don't loop over it. That iteration pattern (for x in state.read()) is only correct for BagStateSpec, which does return an iterable of buffered elements. Check your DoFn's process() method for a stray for-loop or unpacking (e.g. a, b = state.read()) against the ReadModifyWriteStateSpec cell rather than the BagStateSpec one. Since the exact process() body got cut off, the general fix is: only ever consume each state spec the way its type dictates - scalar read/write for ReadModifyWriteStateSpec, iteration only for BagStateSpec - and make sure on_timer isn't treating the EMA float as a windowed collection when emitting it downstream.
